newsitem.title: JAPAN: MOTOR RACING-CHAMPION HILL REALISES CHERISHED DREAM.
newsitem.headline: MOTOR RACING-CHAMPION HILL REALISES CHERISHED DREAM.

text.p: Damon Hill achieved his most cherished ambition on Sunday when he emulated his father Graham's achievement of winning the world drivers' championship against all the odds and after a career littered with setbacks.
Hill, who is being dropped by his triumphant Williams team and replaced by German Heinz-Harald Frentzen, drove to glory with a masterful victory in the Japanese Grand Prix.
It marked the end of six years of consistent progress from test driver to champion and followed two near-misses and some bitter criticism from paddock observers.

For Hill, an ordinary family man, whose understated approach to the fame of Formula One has made him an underestimated star, it was a day of extraordinary emotions to cap a lifetime of extraordinary events and sadness.
After the race the 36-year-old driver thanked his family and friends, and particularly his wife Georgie, for their support through the year.
"I can hardly wait to get back to my children but it is especially Georgie I would like to thank for this championship," he said.
"She has stood by me the whole way and has been a tremendous strength to me throughout the season and all the time I have been racing in Formula One."
Hill, the son of a double world champion driver, climbed to the top against his mother's wishes and by digging deep into his reserves of determination and ambition from the age 15.
He had a privileged childhood as the son of Graham Hill, world champion in 1962 and 1968, attending private schools and going on exotic holidays.
But he lost all that when his father was killed in a light plane crash at Elstree, England, in 1975.

It had catastrophic financial effects on the family, leaving Graham's wife Bette, daughters Samantha and Brigitte and son Damon to grow up in the glare of fame without the support a husband and father and without the wealth he had accumulated.
Insurance claims arising from the accident decimated the value of Hill's estate. For Damon it meant a life of challenges if he was to deliver achievements to match those of his father.
Damon had his first opportunity to drive a car when he sat at the wheel on his father's knee at the age of five -- an experience which stimulated a lifelong addiction to speed.
But he began his racing career on two wheels rather than four following a spell of work in London as a motorcycle messenger during which he was a member of a punk rock band.

His career as a motorcycle racer began in 1979 and he won 40 races on a Yamaha. He switched to Formula Ford racing in the second half of 1984 after attending a racing school in France at the request of his mother.
He graduated through Formula Ford, British Formula Three and the international F3000 championship with a variety of teams before becoming test driver for Williams in 1991.

Hill kept the job in 1992 when he also raced in Formula One for the first time for the now-defunct Brabham team. He qualified for his first grand prix, the British, at Silverstone that year and finished 16th.

The following year Hill was offered the number two drive at Williams alongside Frenchman Alain Prost and finished third in the title race after overcoming a nervous start to score a hat-trick of successive victories in Hungary, Belgium and Italy.
In 1994, he was partnered by triple world champion Ayrton Senna of Brazil who was killed at the San Marino Grand Prix early in the season.
This left Hill as team leader and he responded with dignity in adverse circumstances.
After battling all season with Germany's Michael Schumacher Hill was the victim of a dramatic collision in the final race in Australia and missed the title by a single point.

He was second again in 1995 in less controversial but far more disappointing circumstances. Hill determined to overcome this by training and organising himself better than ever in the winter after moving home from England to Dublin.
There he and his family have lived away from the bright lights giving him a chance to protect his wife and three children from unnecessary publicity.
His oldest son Oliver, born with Down's Syndrome, needed special care and attention. Hill's devotion earned him worldwide respect.

This respect, coupled with the driver's dry and self-effacing wit, his principles and his ill-at-ease appearances in the glare of the cameras, won him a vast army of supporters whose sympathies increased when he was dropped by Williams three weeks ago.

For the majority of his fans, Hill's success is that of an ordinary man in overcoming the obstacles of life in pursuit of a dream which he has achieved without losing his sense of humour or his manners.
